prompt.context: Two of your business school classmates decided to open a video rental store near the HBS campus despite trends suggesting otherwise. Their first two years met unprecedented success — they bought matching Porsches and a townhouse in Beacon Hill. However, about 12 months later, despite two and a half years of dramatic profit and revenue growth, profits have dramatically fallen. They call you (an associate at a prominent strategy consulting firm) and say: 'We don't know what happened and our mortgage and car payments are getting tougher to meet. Can you help us?'
prompt.question: What do you think the problem is?

clarifying_info.q: Have costs increased or have revenues declined?
Why is cost probably not the main issue?
clarifying_info.a: Video rental is a high fixed-cost business — rent, videos, and labor are all largely fixed relative to rental revenue. Profits are therefore highly susceptible to revenue changes (capacity utilization).

clarifying_info.q: Has management changed the price of videos?
How would you determine whether the revenue decline is due to fewer customers or fewer rentals per customer?
clarifying_info.a: The security system likely has a door counter for traffic; register receipts show videos rented per day. Comparing this year vs. last year reveals whether it is a traffic problem or a share-of-wallet problem.

clarifying_info.q: Has a new video store opened in the area?
Has a new movie theatre opened?

framework: Diagnose the P&L: determine whether the profit decline stems from a revenue drop or a cost increase
Decompose revenue: Price × Volume (number of rentals)
Decompose volume: store traffic (number of customers) vs. rentals per customer (share of wallet)
Identify root cause of traffic decline: macro factors vs. competitive situation
Expand the competitive set: define the client's business correctly (home movie entertainment, not just video rental stores)
Hypothesize specific competitive threats within the redefined market (delivery, cable, PPV, Video-on-Demand)

questions.prompt: Revenues have declined and prices are unchanged. What are the two possible drivers of lower revenue volume?
questions.guidance: Revenue = Price × Quantity. Since price is unchanged, volume must be down. Volume can fall because (1) fewer customers visit the store (traffic problem) or (2) existing customers rent fewer videos per visit (share-of-wallet problem). Candidate should distinguish these because they point to different root causes and fixes.

questions.prompt: How would you figure out whether the issue is a traffic problem or a share-of-wallet problem?
questions.guidance: Use operational data already available in the store: (1) door/security counter for foot traffic year-over-year; (2) register receipts for average videos rented per transaction. Comparing current year vs. prior year on both metrics isolates the driver.

questions.prompt: The data shows traffic has fallen. What are the likely causes, and how do you narrow them down?
questions.guidance: Traffic decline is typically external/market-driven (vs. share-of-wallet, which is internal execution). Two broad buckets: (1) macro factors (economic downturn, demographic shift) — candidate should note video rental is relatively inelastic to mild economic changes; (2) competitive situation — new entrants stealing customers. Candidate should immediately probe: new video store nearby? New movie theatre? When both are ruled out, candidate must broaden the competitive frame.

questions.prompt: No new video store and no new movie theatre have opened. What next?
questions.guidance: This is the pivotal insight moment. The interviewer prompts: 'What business is your client really in?' The correct answer is the home movie entertainment business — not just brick-and-mortar video rental. The full competitive set therefore includes any channel that delivers movies to the home: mail/delivery DVD services, cable movie channels, pay-per-view, and emerging Video-on-Demand technology. The hypothesis is that one or more of these substitutes has grown rapidly, shrinking the addressable market for in-store rentals.

brainstorming.prompt: If the traffic decline is confirmed to be driven by home-entertainment substitutes, what specific competitive threats should the client investigate?

categories.name: Physical delivery substitutes
ideas: Mail-order DVD rental services (e.g., early Netflix model)
Kiosk rentals (e.g., Redbox) placed in convenient locations

categories.name: Macro and demographic
ideas: Economic pressure reducing discretionary entertainment spend overall

recommendation: The root cause of the profit decline is most likely a structural market-size contraction driven by home-entertainment substitutes — particularly emerging on-demand and delivery-based movie options — that have redefined the competitive landscape beyond brick-and-mortar video stores.

The client should validate this hypothesis by quantifying traffic loss against the growth of local cable PPV, VOD, and delivery services, then evaluate whether to diversify into complementary services or accept a structurally smaller addressable market.
risks: If the substitute services continue to grow (as historical trends suggest), the in-store rental model faces long-term secular decline regardless of operational improvements.
Any strategic pivot (e.g., adding game rentals, concessions, or online presence) requires capital the owners may not have given their current financial strain.
next_steps: Confirm hypothesis by cross-referencing traffic data with adoption rates of VOD/delivery services in the local area.
Assess whether the store can reposition as a niche curator (specialty/foreign films) to defend a segment less exposed to mainstream digital substitutes.
Evaluate cost structure for potential right-sizing if the addressable market has permanently contracted.
